lessons.title: Building a Pitch Deck That Gets a Second Meeting

children.text: A partner at a Mumbai fund opens your deck between two meetings, on a phone, in a car. You have maybe three minutes and eleven slides before a decision gets made: reply, forward to a colleague, or leave it. Your deck is not a business plan and it is not a document that wins the investment. It has exactly one job, which is to earn the next conversation. Everything in this lesson follows from that.

body.text: A pitch deck does not have to prove you will win. It has to make a busy, sceptical person curious enough to spend an hour with you. Clarity beats completeness, and evidence beats adjectives.

children.text: The Eleven Slides, and the Question Each One Answers

body.caption: A standard seed and Series A deck structure

cells: 1. Title and one-liner
What do you do, in one sentence my mother would understand?
Jargon, or a tagline that could describe fifty companies
2. Problem
Who is hurting, how badly, and how do you know?
A problem asserted with no evidence that anyone pays to solve it
3. Solution and product
What exactly did you build, and what does using it look like?
Vision language with no screenshot or demo of what exists today
4. Why now
What changed recently that makes this possible today?
No trigger, which suggests others tried this and failed
5. Market
How large can this realistically become?
A top-down number lifted from a consultant's report
6. Traction
Is anything actually working?
Cumulative charts, vanity counts, or a chart with no axis labels
7. Business model and unit economics
How do you make money on one customer?
Revenue with no mention of what it costs to serve
8. Go to market
How do you reach the next 1,000 customers?
Listing every possible channel instead of the one that works
9. Competition
Why does anyone choose you?
A tick-box grid where you have every tick and rivals have none
10. Team
Why is this the team that wins?
Logos of past employers with no link to this problem
11. The ask
How much, on what terms, and what does it buy?
An amount with no milestones attached to it

body.text: Order matters less than most founders think, with one exception. If you have real traction, move it to slide 3. An investor who sees ₹1.4 crore of revenue growing 12% a month will read your problem slide generously. An investor who has waded through four slides of vision before reaching any evidence has already started composing the polite no.

children.text: If a partner cannot repeat what you do to a colleague, your deck stops moving inside the fund. The test is simple: one sentence, no jargon, naming the customer and the outcome.

columns.label: Weak
points: Nobody knows who the customer is
Nobody knows what gets bought or sold

columns.label: Strong
points: "We help onion traders in Nashik sell to buyers in six states and get paid within 48 hours"
Specific enough to be wrong, which makes it credible
A partner can repeat it after one read

body.title: Pick the opening line
body.question: Four founders open their decks with one sentence. Which one earns the most attention from an investor reading on a phone?
options: "We are building the operating system for Bharat's next billion users"
"We are a full-stack, vertically integrated, technology-first platform for the unorganised sector"
"Diagnostics labs in tier 2 cities lose 30% of samples to manual errors. We give them a ₹4,000-a-month app that tracks every sample from collection to report, and 62 labs now use it daily"
"Our mission is to transform healthcare in India through innovation and empathy"
body.explanation: The third names the customer, the pain, the product, the price and the evidence, all in two sentences. The others could be any company in any year. Ambition is fine on a later slide, but the first line has to be specific enough to check.

children.text: Build the Market Slide From the Bottom Up

markDefs.definition: Estimating market size by counting real customers and multiplying by what each realistically pays you, rather than taking a share of a large published industry number.

children.text: Every second deck claims a market of a few lakh crore, and every investor discounts it instantly. A

is more persuasive precisely because it is smaller and checkable. For the diagnostics software above: roughly 1 lakh diagnostics labs in India, of which about 30,000 are in the cities you serve, at ₹4,000 a month. That is 30,000 × ₹48,000 a year, or ₹144 crore of realistic annual revenue opportunity. An investor can argue with each input, which is exactly the conversation you want.

body.latex: \text{Reachable market} = \text{Number of realistic customers} \times \text{Annual revenue per customer}
body.caption: Two inputs an investor can test, instead of one number they cannot

body.title: Build it yourself
body.prompt: A startup sells billing software to chemists at ₹1,500 a month. It can realistically reach 40,000 chemist shops across the states where it operates. What is the reachable annual market, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹1,500 × 12 = ₹18,000 a year per shop. 40,000 × ₹18,000 = ₹72,00,00,000, which is ₹72 crore. A bottom-up number like this invites a real discussion about how many shops are genuinely reachable and whether ₹1,500 a month holds, which is exactly the conversation a top-down market slide never starts.

children.text: The Traction Slide Is the Deck

This is the slide investors screenshot and share internally. Three rules. Show monthly figures, not cumulative ones, because cumulative charts only go up and everyone knows it. Label the axes and state the metric precisely, so revenue means revenue and not GMV. And do not hide the bad month, because diligence will find it and your explanation is far more convincing when you volunteer it.

body.title: Monthly net revenue (₹ lakh), last 9 months

body.text: April dipped, and that is fine. A one-line footnote saying "April: we paused paid spend to rebuild checkout" turns a weak month into evidence that you understand your own business. Founders who smooth charts into perfect curves get asked for raw data, and the conversation never recovers.

body.title: What to put on the traction slide when you have no revenue

children.text: Pre-revenue is normal at pre-seed and early seed. The slide still has to show that something real happened, so use evidence of demand rather than a promise of it.
Signed pilots or letters of intent, with the customer names and what they agreed to.
Usage from a free or beta product: weekly active users, tasks completed, messages sent, with the retention curve.
A waitlist, but only with conversion evidence: how many of the first 100 invited actually activated.
Findings from customer discovery: 40 interviews, what you learned, and what you changed because of it.
One paying customer at ₹5,000 a month tells an investor more than a 50,000-name waitlist, because somebody chose to part with money.

Most founders write "raising ₹8 crore" and stop. That answers nothing. The ask slide should show what the money buys and what the company will have proved by the time it runs out, because that is the case for your next round.

body.caption: Use of funds for an ₹8 crore seed round, with an 18-month plan

cells: Engineering and product
Six engineers and a product lead to ship the billing and reports module
Sales and customer success
Two city teams, taking labs live from 62 to about 400
Marketing and channel
Distributor partnerships and a referral programme
Compliance, audit and legal
Audited accounts, contracts and data security certification
Buffer
Roughly 12% cushion, because plans slip
Total
18 months of runway, ending at about ₹6 crore of ARR

body.label: How much to raise
body.value: Enough for 18 to 24 months, plus a buffer
body.context: Raise for the milestones that make the next round obvious, not for a round number. Too little and you are back in the market before the evidence exists. Too much at an inflated valuation and you set a bar the next round has to clear.

stats.label: The send deck
stats.context: Read alone with no narrator, so every slide has a full headline sentence

stats.label: The present deck
stats.context: You are the narrative, the slides carry only the evidence

stats.label: The intro email
stats.context: One-liner, traction, the ask, why this investor, deck attached

stats.label: The appendix
stats.context: Cohorts, pricing, competition detail and compliance, for the people who dig

body.text: Never send financial projections, customer contracts or detailed cap tables with a first email. Share a deck, and put the rest in a data room you control access to, after the first real conversation. Decks get forwarded, and in India they often reach a competitor's investor within weeks.

body.title: Why is nobody replying?
body.scenario: Ritu has sent her deck to 40 investors over six weeks. Eleven opened it, three took calls, none progressed. Her deck: slide 1 is a mission statement about empowering small businesses, slides 2 to 5 describe the product's features, slide 6 shows a ₹2.4 lakh crore addressable market, slide 7 is a cumulative chart of registered users rising to 40,000, slide 8 is a competitor grid where she has ticks in every row, slide 9 lists the team's college and employer logos, and slide 10 says "Raising ₹10 crore". Her actual business: 240 shops pay ₹2,000 a month, revenue has grown from ₹1.9 lakh to ₹4.8 lakh a month over the last seven months, and 88% of shops that joined six months ago are still paying.
body.prompt: Diagnose the deck and say what you would change first.
body.modelAnswer:
The business is far better than the deck, which is the whole problem. Her three strongest facts are buried or missing.
What is wrong:
1. The real traction is absent. ₹4.8 lakh of monthly revenue, up about 2.5 times in seven months, and 88% six-month retention. None of it appears. Registered users as a cumulative chart is a vanity metric and investors discount it automatically.
2. Slide 1 says nothing checkable. "Empowering small businesses" could be anyone.
3. Four product feature slides answer a question nobody asked yet.
4. The market number is top-down and unbelievable. Bottom-up, 240 shops at ₹24,000 a year against a reachable base she can actually name would be stronger.
5. The competitor grid with all ticks destroys trust. Every investor knows rivals do some things better.
6. "Raising ₹10 crore" with no use of funds or milestones gives nobody a reason to engage.
What to change first: rebuild slides 1 to 3. Slide 1 becomes "240 kirana shops pay us ₹2,000 a month to manage billing and stock. Revenue has grown from ₹1.9 lakh to ₹4.8 lakh a month since March, and 88% of our six-month cohort still pays." Slide 2 the problem with evidence from those shops, slide 3 the monthly revenue and retention charts. Compress the product to one slide, rebuild the market bottom-up, make the competition slide honest, and end with an ask tied to milestones. Then send it to 15 well-matched investors, not 40 random ones.

body.title: Pre-send deck audit
steps: Can someone outside your industry repeat your one-liner after reading it once?
Does every slide headline state a conclusion, rather than label a topic?
Is traction shown monthly, with labelled axes and the metric named precisely?
Is the market built bottom-up from customer counts and prices you can defend?
Does the competition slide admit at least one thing a rival does better?
Does the ask state the amount, the runway it buys and the milestones it funds?
Is every number in the deck identical to the numbers in your data room and your accounts?
Is it readable on a phone, with no text smaller than what you can read at arm's length?

body.title: The slide founders get wrong
body.textWithBlank: An ask slide should state the amount, the runway it buys, and the ___ of funds, so the investor can see exactly what the money is meant to prove.
body.explanation: Use of funds turns a number into a plan. It also tells the investor whether you have thought about the milestones that will make your next round straightforward.

cards.definition: A single jargon-free sentence naming the customer and the outcome, specific enough that a partner can repeat it.
Realistic customer count multiplied by annual revenue per customer, instead of a share of a published industry figure.
The version read without you present, where every slide headline states its own conclusion.
How the money will be spent and what milestones it buys, shown on the ask slide.
A controlled folder of financials, contracts, cap table and compliance documents, shared after a first real conversation.
Detailed backup slides on cohorts, pricing and competition, for investors who want to dig deeper.

points: The deck has one job: earn the next conversation. It is not a business plan and it will not win the investment on its own.
Eleven slides are enough. Each answers one question, and if you have real traction, move it to slide 3.
Write the one-liner first. If a partner cannot repeat it internally, your deck stops moving inside the fund.
Build the market bottom-up: realistic customers multiplied by annual revenue per customer, so the inputs can be argued with.
Show traction monthly with labelled axes, and volunteer the bad month with a one-line explanation.
The ask slide needs the amount, the runway it buys and the milestones it funds. Raise for 18 to 24 months plus a buffer.
Send the deck, not the data room. Projections, contracts and cap tables come after a first real conversation.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Deck lengths, slide counts and runway guidance are common market practice that varies by investor and stage, not rules. Ritu's company, the diagnostics and chemist software examples and all figures are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
